newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani doctor sees profit in healing business.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani doctor sees profit in healing business.

text.p: Zaheer Ahmed, an expatriate Pakistani leading a team of doctors-turned-entrepreneurs, sees healthcare as a corporate opportunity in Pakistan, where state resources are unable to meet growing demands.

Ahmed, president of Shifa International Hospitals Ltd, has set up a 100-bed private hospital in Islamabad managed by mainly U.S.-trained Pakistani doctors. He said private health care was the only solution for countries such as Pakistan.

"This country cannot afford any more health care unless you have more private health care available," Ahmed said in an interview with Reuters. "The government should be involved in regulating this sector, but unfortunately it is not."
Ahmed said the Islamabad hospital, started in December 1993, was now breaking even and could soon turn a healthy profit from its large and expanding base of 65,000 patients.
Affluent, health-conscious Pakistanis like Shifa's American design, sparkling clean corridors, modern equipment and computers used for anything from registration to diagnosis.

The company's 10-rupee share was trading at only 4.85 rupees on October 27, but dealers attributed its under-par performance to a general depression in Pakistani stock markets and the unfamiliarity of health sector enterprises to many investors.

"It is the first venture in the health sector," Agha Arshad, an Islamabad-based stocks analyst said. "Investors do not know its profitability, they have no experience of its management and it is an out-of-the-market (illiquid) scrip," he added.
"Your brokers, financial firms have very little knowledge of hospital functioning, they do not understand that hospitals cannot come into profit before five years," Ahmed said.

"It is a solid company, it is a solid return and hospitals can become a cash cow. Now we have developed a base, which is just a start. My forecast is that in the next few years we will be making billions of rupees," Ahmed said.
He said monthly revenue had risen to about 21 million rupees ($522,000) from two to three million rupees at the beginning.

Shifa's paid-up capital 500 million rupees contributed by 458 sponsors. Ahmed himself persuaded most of them to sink money in the venture or return to Pakistan from the United States and other foreign countries to work at Shifa.

"Most of them are from outside Pakistan. I personally went to people in the United States and Saudi Arabia and it took months for me to convince people to leave United States and ask them to invest their hard currency over here," Ahmed said.

Ahmed, who says he is motivated partly by patriotism, said he had persuaded 75 families to come back to Pakistan in connection with the project. About 40 returning doctors had taken jobs at Shifa, as well as 35 nurses and paramedical staff.
"Their number is increasing -- two to three every month -- and this process of reverse migration will continue," he said.
Ahmed said those who left the luxury and comfort of America had not returned expecting to make lots of money, but to share in a venture that would ultimately serve their country.
The hospital began admitting in-patients in December 1993 and now has 100 beds. This is to be expanded to 300 beds in the next five years and to 600 within 10 years.
Ahmed said future plans include building a medical college and a nursing college as independent companies by the end of 1997 and a Shifa University of Medical Sciences by 2000.
The company has already started opening small private clinics in other Pakistani cities.
